# Diseases of the vitreous body

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ophthalmology > Lens and vitreous body > Diseases of the vitreous body*

[Original Article Link](/library/rO0fFT)

---

## Summary

The <u>vitreous body</u> is the transparent, gelatinous substance that fills the space of the <u>eye</u> between <u>lens</u> and <u>retina</u>. It allows light to pass from the <u>lens</u> to the <u>retina</u> and normally has enough mass to maintain the eyeball's spherical shape and counteract <u>retinal detachment</u>. This article covers the most common diseases of the <u>vitreous body</u>, including <u>posterior vitreous detachment</u> and <u>vitreous hemorrhage</u>.
<u>Posterior vitreous detachment</u> is the separation of the <u>posterior</u> <u>vitreous</u> cortex from the internal limiting membrane of the <u>retina</u>. Etiologies include age-related degeneration of the <u>vitreous</u> tissue, elongation of the ocular bulb, and <u>eye</u> injuries. Patients are usually asymptomatic, but may complain of <u>floaters</u> and <u>photopsia</u>. <u>Vitreous detachment</u> is confirmed on <u>slit lamp examination</u>. Asymptomatic individuals do not require treatment. Symptomatic individuals with retinal injury (e.g., retinal tears/holes, <u>retinal detachment</u>) require prompt treatment with, e.g., <u>laser photocoagulation</u>.
<u>Vitreous hemorrhage</u> is the extravasation of blood into the <u>vitreous body</u> and its adjacent structures. It can be caused by trauma and a variety of diseases, e.g., <u>proliferative diabetic retinopathy</u>, <u>posterior vitreous detachment</u>, and tumors. Clinical features include painless sudden onset of unilateral <u>floaters</u> and/or visual loss. <u>Slit lamp examination</u> confirms the presence blood in the <u>vitreous body</u>. Initially, a wait-and-see approach is recommended, since the condition typically resolves spontaneously. However, if the <u>retina</u> is affected or severe disease progression occurs, <u>vitrectomy</u> is indicated.

---

## Posterior vitreous detachment

* Definition: detachment of the <u>posterior</u> <u>vitreous</u> cortex from the internal limiting membrane of the <u>retina</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak <u>incidence</u> between 45–65 years of age

* Etiology

* Age-related degenerative <u>liquefaction</u> and collapse of the <u>vitreous body</u> (most common cause)

* <u>Myopia</u>

* <u>Eye</u> injury

* <u>Chorioretinitis</u>

* <u>Aphakia</u> (absence of the <u>lens</u>)

* Clinical features

* Patients are usually asymptomatic

* Photopsia: A sudden and brief perception of bright <u>flashes of light</u> that often start in one area of the <u>visual field</u>. It usually is unilateral and occurs in the dark or with closed eyes.

* <u>Floaters</u>

* Diagnostics
* <u>Slit lamp examination</u>: detached <u>posterior</u> surface of the <u>vitreous</u> becomes visible as thin irregular ring (Weiss ring)

* Treatment

* Treatment is not necessary in patients without retinal injury and/or patients in whom symptoms resolve

* Symptomatic patients with retinal injury require prompt treatment (see complication below)

* Complications

* Retinal tears/holes

* Rhegmatogenous <u>retinal detachment</u>

* <u>Vitreous hemorrhage</u>





> [!WARNING]
> The sudden onset of <u>floaters</u> and/or the perception of flashes require urgent examination of the ocular fundus to rule out retinal injury!

## Vitreous hemorrhage

* Definition: the extravasation of blood in and around the <u>vitreous body</u>

* Etiology: 

* Rupture of neovascular vessels in <u>ischemic</u> changes of the <u>retina</u> 

* <u>Proliferative diabetic retinopathy</u> (most common cause)

* <u>Sickle cell</u> <u>retinopathy</u>

* <u>Ocular ischemic syndrome</u>

* <u>Retinopathy of prematurity</u>

* <u>Retinal vein occlusion</u>

* <u>Age-related macular degeneration</u>

* Rupture of physiological vessels

* Lesions of the <u>retina</u> in symptomatic <u>posterior vitreous detachment</u>

* Retinal tear

* Blunt or penetrating traumatic injuries to the <u>sclera</u> or <u>retina</u>

* <u>Increased intracranial pressure</u>, e.g., in <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u> (<u>Terson syndrome</u>)

* Hemorrhage from an adjacent site

* Retinal macroaneurysm

* Choroidal <u>neovascularization</u>

* Tumors

* Clinical features

* Sudden onset of symptoms: usually unilateral and painless

* <u>Floaters</u> and/or visual loss: typically worse after <u>sleep</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Slit lamp examination</u> 

* Blood between the <u>posterior</u> <u>vitreous</u> base and internal limiting membrane

* Can determine the source of <u>vitreous hemorrhage</u> (e.g., retinal <u>neovascularization</u>)

* Ocular B-scan <u>ultrasonography</u> if blood completely obscures the <u>posterior</u> segment of the <u>eye</u>

* Treatment

* Since hemorrhage may resolve spontaneously, a wait-and-see approach is recommended at the beginning of treatment.

* Treatment of the underlying cause

* If severe disease progression/<u>retinal detachment</u> occurs: vitrectomy
* Surgical removal of the <u>vitreous humor</u> and temporary filling of the <u>eye</u> with liquid silicone, saline, or gas to replace the <u>vitreous humor</u>

* <u>Photocoagulation</u> for retinal breaks or proliferative retinal vascular disease

## Preretinal subhyaloid hemorrhage

* Definition: hemorrhage between the <u>retina</u> and the <u>posterior</u> <u>vitreous</u> membrane

* Etiology

* Microangiopathy/<u>neovascularization</u> (e.g., in <u>proliferative diabetic retinopathy</u>)

* Disorders of <u>hemostasis</u> and <u>fibrinolysis</u>

* Clinical features

* Sudden onset of black opacities and/or visual loss

* <u>Hyphema</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Slit lamp examination</u>

* Well-demarcated boat-shaped hemorrhage in the <u>posterior</u> <u>eye</u> segment

* Blood in the potential space between the internal limiting membrane and the <u>retina</u>

* Ocular B-scan <u>ultrasonography</u> if blood completely obscures the <u>posterior</u> segment of the <u>eye</u>

* Treatment

* Laser hyaloidotomy: opening of the <u>vitreous body</u>'s hyaloid membrane → blood distribution by <u>diffusion</u>

* Pars plana <u>vitrectomy</u>: surgical procedure in which the <u>vitreous</u> gel is removed from the <u>eye</u> by introducing the instruments through the pars plana





![Preretinal subhyaloid hemorrhage](media/mip5ixo0m2pf9s73y3ed3irt.jpg)

## Floaters

* Definition: deposits in the <u>vitreous body</u> perceived as spots or strings drifting through the <u>visual field</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[4]](/library/KGXUZ-)

* Peak age: > 50 years

* <u>♀</u> = <u>♂</u>

* Etiology [[5]](/library/TGX6Az)

* Primary <u>floaters</u>: <u>collagen fibrils</u> originating from within the <u>vitreous body</u>

* Weakened vitreoretinal adhesion → <u>posterior vitreous detachment</u> (most common cause)

* Degenerative processes (e.g., <u>liquefaction</u>, aggregation of <u>collagen fibrils</u>) in the <u>vitreous humor</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u>: <u>myopia</u>, <u>Stickler syndrome</u>, <u>Marfan syndrome</u>

* Secondary <u>floaters</u>: protein, <u>amyloid</u>, or cell debris originating from outside the <u>vitreous body</u>

* <u>Retinal detachment</u>, retinal tear

* <u>Vitreous hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Posterior uveitis</u>

* <u>Eye</u> <u>tumor</u> (e.g., ocular <u>melanoma</u>)

* Intraocular foreign body

* Clinical features

* Perception of opacities of various shapes and sizes (e.g., spots, strings, filamentous structures)

* Follow <u>eye movements</u> quickly

* Drift slowly across the <u>visual field</u> when the <u>eye</u> is still

* Tend to move away when gazed at directly

* Appear more intensely against bright lighting and monochromatic areas (e.g., white paper, blue sky)

* Symptoms indicating secondary <u>floaters</u>

* Sudden increase in/occurrence of <u>floaters</u>, especially if accompanied by <u>photopsia</u> and/or <u>vision loss</u>

* Showers of <u>floaters</u>: the sudden appearance of innumerable <u>floaters</u> (perceived as multiple black spots)

* Diagnostics

* Ocular <u>ultrasound</u>: especially useful to rule out secondary <u>floaters</u> and quantify primary <u>floaters</u>

* Visualization of the entire <u>vitreous body</u>

* Assessment of the severity of <u>floaters</u> is possible by measuring <u>vitreous</u> opacities, which are non-sight-threatening but may cause visual disturbance and, subsequently, affect quality of life.

* The diagnosis of the disease condition causing secondary <u>floaters</u> typically involves <u>slit lamp examination</u> or <u>ophthalmoscopy</u>.

* Treatment [[5]](/library/TGX6Az)

* Patient education on symptoms indicating secondary <u>floaters</u>

* Primary <u>floaters</u>

* First line: observation and reassurance

* <u>Vitrectomy</u>

* Laser vitreolysis

* Secondary <u>floaters</u>: treatment of underlying disease (discussed in respective articles)





> [!WARNING]
> A severe increase in <u>floaters</u> accompanied by <u>photopsia</u> is a typical symptom of acute <u>posterior vitreous detachment</u>, which bears a risk of retinal tearing and <u>retinal detachment</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Showers of <u>floaters</u> indicate the presence of free cells in the <u>vitreous</u> and are usually associated with <u>vitreous hemorrhage</u>.
